Fast Fourier Transform for Rates

Source: vignettes/fft.Rmd
fft.Rmd

In this vignette we describe the mathematical details of how the convolution integrals in the expressions for the encounter rate and for the mortality rate are calculated with the help of Fast Fourier Transform (FFT).

Conservation Equations

The model dynamics are described by the McKendrick-von Foerster equation for the species number densities \(N_i(w)\) and the resource number density \(N_R(w)\).

The Convolution Integrals

The encounter rate \(E_i(w)\) of a predator of species \(i\) and weight \(w\) is given by \[ E_i(w) = \gamma_i(w) \int \left( \theta_{ip} N_R(w_p) + \sum_{j} \theta_{ij} N_j(w_p) \right) \phi_i(w,w_p) w_p \, dw_p. \] The first term in the integral is the contribution from the resource and the second term is the contribution from the fish prey. \(\gamma_i(w)\) is the search volume, \(\theta_{ij}\) is the interaction matrix, and \(\phi_i(w,w_p)\) is the predation kernel.

The predation rate \(P_j(w_p)\) on a prey of species \(j\) and size \(w_p\) is given by \[ P_j(w_p) = \sum_i \int \phi_i(w,w_p) (1-f_i(w)) \gamma_i(w) N_i(w) \, dw. \] Here \(f_i(w)\) is the feeding level of the predator.

Discretization on Logarithmic Grid

We use a logarithmic grid of weights \(w_k = w_1 \beta^{k-1}\) for \(k=1,\dots,K\), where \(\beta = 10^{\Delta x}\). The integral over prey size \(w_p\) transforms into a sum over grid indices \(k\). Assuming the predation kernel depends only on the predator/prey mass ratio \(w/w_p\), i.e., \(\phi_i(w,w_p) = \tilde{\phi}_i(w/w_p)\), and converting to log-space \(x = \log_\beta w\), the integrals become convolutions.

Let \(x_k = \log_\beta w_k = x_1 + (k-1)\). The term \(\phi_i(w_n, w_k) = \tilde{\phi}_i(\beta^{n-k})\).

Fast Fourier Transform Implementation

The evaluation of these convolution sums is computationally expensive if done directly (\(\mathcal{O}(K^2)\)). By using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), we can reduce the complexity to \(\mathcal{O}(K \log K)\).

Encounter Rate

The integral for the encounter rate can be written as a convolution of the available prey energy density with the predation kernel. Let \(A(w_p) = (\theta_{ip} N_R(w_p) + \sum_{j} \theta_{ij} N_j(w_p)) w_p\). The discretized encounter rate (ignoring coefficients) is roughly \[ E[n] = \sum_k \tilde{\phi}[n-k] A[k] \] In mizer, we define ft_pred_kernel_e as the FFT of the predation kernel. The available energy is calculated, transformed via FFT, multiplied by ft_pred_kernel_e, and then inverse transformed. In a model of defaults edition 3 or later, both the kernel and the available energy are first padded with zeros, for the reason explained in Avoiding wrap-around below.

mizerEncounter() hands this to convolve_pred_kernel(), which does the following, where no_k is the length of the padded grid (equal to no_w_full in a model of an earlier edition) and idx_sp picks out the fish sizes:

# prey is species x w_full; place it on the padded grid
prey_padded <- matrix(0, nrow = no_k, ncol = no_sp)
prey_padded[1:no_w_full, ] <- t(prey)
avail_energy <- Re(mvfft(t(params@ft_pred_kernel_e) * mvfft(prey_padded),
                         inverse = TRUE)) / no_k
avail_energy <- t(avail_energy[idx_sp, ])

Predation Rate

Similarly, the predation rate is a convolution of the predator density (scaled by search volume and feeding level) with the predation kernel. However, there is a slight difference in the indexing because the integral is over predator sizes \(w\), whereas the kernel is usually defined in terms of predator/prey ratio. \[ P(w_p) = \int \tilde{\phi}(w/w_p) D(w) dw \] where \(D(w) = (1-f(w)) \gamma(w) N(w)\). In terms of indices: \[ P[k] = \sum_n \tilde{\phi}[n-k] D[n] \] To compute this as a standard convolution \(P[k] = \sum_n \psi[k-n] D[n]\), we need to define a reversed kernel \(\psi[m] = \tilde{\phi}[-m]\). This is why setPredKernel() calculates ft_pred_kernel_p using a reversed version of the kernel.

# R/setPredKernel.R
phi_p <- rep(0, no_k)
phi_p[(no_k - no_w_full + 2):no_k] <- phi[no_w_full:2]
ft_pred_kernel_p[i, ] <- fft(phi_p)

The phi_p construction reverses the kernel and places the negative offsets \(-m\) at the end of the padded grid, at index no_k - m + 1, to suit the FFT definition of convolution.

Higher-order quadrature: bin-integrated kernels

Why the naive scheme is only first order

The convolution sums above are quadrature approximations of the encounter and predation integrals. As written in the introductory sections they amount to a rectangle rule: the species and resource densities are treated as piecewise constant across each size bin (the finite-volume cell average), and the predation kernel is point-sampled at the grid node, i.e. the term for the pair of bins \((n,k)\) uses the single value \(\tilde\phi_i(\beta^{n-k})\) together with the left-edge measure \(w_k\,dw_k\).

Three things make this only first-order accurate:

  1. The kernel is replaced by its value at one point of the bin instead of its average over the bin.
  2. The size variable \(w_p\) that multiplies the kernel in the encounter integral is frozen at the left edge \(w_k\) of the bin, even though \(w_p\) varies by a factor \(\beta = 10^{\Delta x}\) across the bin.
  3. The factor \((1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\) that multiplies the kernel in the predation integral is frozen at the left edge \(w_n\) of the predator bin, even though the search volume alone varies by a factor \(\beta^{q_i}\) across the bin.

All three errors are \(O(\Delta x)\) and all three come from how the smooth factors of the integrand are sampled — not from the piecewise-constant representation of the densities, which is the genuinely finite-volume part of the scheme. The third is easy to overlook, because in the encounter integral the very same search volume \(\gamma_i(w)\) is correctly a point value: there it depends only on the predator size \(w\) at which the rate is evaluated and sits outside the integral. In the predation integral the roles are reversed, the integral runs over predator size, and \((1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\) is a function of the integration variable.

The fix: integrate the kernel over each log-bin

Because the kernel depends only on the predator/prey mass ratio, we can remove both errors by keeping the densities piecewise constant but evaluating the remaining kernel integral over each bin exactly (to the accuracy of a high-order quadrature) instead of by the rectangle rule. This is the finite-volume-consistent quadrature and lifts the rates towards second order.

The grid is logarithmic with bin ratio \(\beta\), so the prey bin \(k\) spans \(w_p \in [w_k, \beta w_k]\). Writing \(w_p = w_k\beta^{s}\) with \(s\in[0,1]\), the exact contribution of prey bin \(k\) to the encounter rate of a predator at \(w_n\) is (with the density held at its cell value) \[ \int_{w_k}^{\beta w_k} \tilde\phi_i(w_n/w_p)\,w_p\,dw_p = w_k^2\,\ln\beta\int_0^1 \tilde\phi_i(\beta^{\,n-k-s})\,\beta^{2s}\,ds . \] The integral depends on \(n\) and \(k\) only through the offset \(m = n-k\), so the convolution structure — and hence the FFT method — is preserved. We therefore replace the point value \(\tilde\phi_i(\beta^{m})\) by the bin-integrated kernel \[ \Phi^{E}_i[m] = \frac{\ln\beta}{\beta-1}\int_0^1 \tilde\phi_i(\beta^{\,m-s})\,\beta^{2s}\,ds . \] The prefactor \(\ln\beta/(\beta-1)\) is chosen so that \(\Phi^E_i[m]\) can be dropped straight into the existing convolution: the prey vector already carries the factor \(w_p\,dw_p = (\beta-1)\,w_k^2\), and \(\Phi^E_i[m]\,(\beta-1)\,w_k^2 = w_k^2\,\ln\beta\int_0^1\tilde\phi_i\,\beta^{2s}\,ds\) reproduces the exact bin contribution. The rate function mizerEncounter() is unchanged; only the stored ft_pred_kernel_e is built from \(\Phi^E_i\) rather than from the point-sampled kernel.

The predation integral runs over predator size. Its integrand \(\tilde\phi_i(w/w_p)\,(1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\,N_i(w)\,dw\) carries one power of \(w\) (from \(dw\)) rather than two, but it also carries the predator’s feeding level and search volume, which vary across the predator bin just as \(w_p\) varies across the prey bin in the encounter. So two factors have to be integrated over the predator bin \(w \in [w_n, \beta w_n]\).

The kernel is integrated in the same way as for the encounter, giving the bin-integrated predation kernel \[ \Phi^{P}_i[m] = \frac{\ln\beta}{\beta-1}\int_0^1 \tilde\phi_i(\beta^{\,m+s})\,\beta^{s}\,ds , \] which replaces \(\tilde\phi_i(\beta^{m})\) in the reversed-kernel construction of ft_pred_kernel_p. The predator vector already carries \(dw = (\beta-1)\,w_n\), which the prefactor cancels.

The factor \((1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\) cannot be folded into the kernel: the feeding level changes at every time step, and a custom search volume need not be a power law. So mizerPredRate() replaces its value at the node by its trapezoidal average over the predator bin, \(\tfrac12\bigl((1-f_i)\gamma_i\big|_{w_n} + (1-f_i)\gamma_i\big|_{\beta w_n}\bigr)\), when it builds the predator vector. The averaging is done only where a predator-bin integral uses the factor: here, and in the predation-diffusion coefficient below. The encounter and the growth rate use the feeding level and the search volume as point values at the node, so the stored rates are not averaged.

There is a second integral hidden in the predation rate. Its convolution output sits at the prey node \(w_p\), but predation mortality enters the finite-volume update as a sink integrated against the prey density over the prey bin, \(\tfrac{1}{\Delta w_p}\int_{\text{bin}}\mu_{\mathrm{pred}}(w_p)\, N(w_p)\,dw_p\). So, exactly as for external mortality and fishing, the rate that enters the mortality wants the prey-bin average of \(P_j(w_p)\), not its value at the prey node. Bin-averaging the convolution output over the prey bin is a trapezoid fold of the (reversed) kernel over adjacent offsets, \[ \bar\Phi^{P}_i[m] = \tfrac12\bigl(\Phi^{P}_i[m] + \Phi^{P}_i[m-1]\bigr), \] because \(\tfrac12\bigl(P_j[w_{p}] + P_j[\beta w_{p}]\bigr) = \sum_n \tfrac12\bigl(\Phi^P_i[n-j] + \Phi^P_i[n-j-1]\bigr)\,Q_i[n]\). Storing \(\mathrm{fft}(\bar\Phi^{P})\) as ft_pred_kernel_p makes getPredRate() come out already prey-bin-averaged, so both mizerPredMort() and mizerResourceMort() (the only consumers, both sinks) get the prey-bin average at no runtime cost and with no change to those two functions. With this the two convolutions are fully bin-consistent: encounter integrates the prey bins, and predation integrates both the predator bins and the prey bins. (Encounter is not prey-bin-averaged on its output, because it feeds the growth flux — a point/face quantity — and is bin-averaged only at the reproduction integral; see vignette("numerical_details").)

Why this is the right weighting

Take the box kernel \(\tilde\phi = 1\) over a bin that lies fully inside the kernel’s support. The encounter weight becomes \[ \Phi^{E}[m] = \frac{\ln\beta}{\beta-1}\int_0^1 \beta^{2s}\,ds = \frac{\beta^2-1}{2(\beta-1)} = \frac{\beta+1}{2}, \] which is exactly the bin average of \(w_p/w_k\) over \([w_k,\beta w_k]\) — the correct finite-volume value — whereas the rectangle rule used \(1\), the value at the left edge. The predation weight, in contrast, evaluates to \(\Phi^{P}[m]=1\): the predation measure \(dw\) is integrated exactly by the original scheme already, so the kernel correction there only accounts for the variation of the kernel shape across the bin. That does not mean the predation integral has no frozen factor. It has one, \((1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\), but that factor lives in the predator vector rather than in the kernel, and is corrected there (item 3 above). As \(\Delta x \to 0\) both \(\ln\beta/(\beta-1)\to 1\) and the integrands tend to their node values, so the bin-integrated kernels reduce to the original point-sampled kernels and the schemes agree in the continuum limit.

Why this makes the rates second order

It is worth being precise about why integrating the kernel over the bin lifts the rates from first to second order, because it relies on what the discrete densities represent. In mizer’s finite-volume scheme each \(N_j\) is the average of the density over the \(j\)-th bin (see vignette("numerical_details")), so the bin average is exact for the zeroth moment, \[ \int_{w_j}^{w_{j+1}} \bigl(N(w_p) - N_j\bigr)\,dw_p = 0 . \] The encounter rate is an integral \(\int N(w_p)\,K(w_p)\,dw_p\) against the smooth weight \(K(w_p) = \tilde\phi_i(w_n/w_p)\,w_p\) (and likewise the predation rate is an integral over predator size against \(K(w)=\tilde\phi_i(w/w_p)\,(1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\)). The bin-integrated scheme replaces \(N\) by its bin average and integrates \(K\) over the bin, so the error contributed by bin \(j\) is \[ \int_{w_j}^{w_{j+1}} \bigl(N(w_p) - N_j\bigr)\,K(w_p)\,dw_p = \int_{w_j}^{w_{j+1}} \bigl(N(w_p) - N_j\bigr)\,\bigl(K(w_p) - \bar K_j\bigr)\,dw_p , \] where the second form uses the zero-mean property to subtract any constant \(\bar K_j\). Both factors vary by \(O(\Delta x)\) across the bin, so the per-bin error is \(O(\Delta x^3)\) and, summed over the \(O(1/\Delta x)\) bins, the total error is \(O(\Delta x^2)\) — second order.

For predation the weight is integrated in two pieces: the kernel exactly at setup, and \((1-f_i)\gamma_i\) by the trapezoid rule at run time. The product of the two bin averages differs from the bin average of the product only by the covariance of the two factors across the bin, \(\tfrac{1}{\Delta w_n}\int (\tilde\phi_i - \bar{\tilde\phi}_i)\bigl((1-f_i)\gamma_i - \overline{(1-f_i)\gamma_i}\bigr)\,dw\). Both factors in that integrand are \(O(\Delta x)\), so the covariance is \(O(\Delta x^2)\) and does not lower the order. The trapezoidal average is itself accurate to \(O(\Delta x^2)\), so the predation rate is second order as well.

The rectangle rule forfeits exactly this cancellation: by point-sampling the smooth factors at the node it does not integrate the smooth weight \(K\) over the bin, which reintroduces an \(O(\Delta x)\) error — the systematic \((\beta+1)/2\) bias seen above. So, given the finite-volume (bin-average) densities, it is the treatment of the whole smooth weight, not only of the kernel, that determines whether the encounter and predation rate quadratures are first or second order. Integrating only the kernel over the bin leaves the predation rate first order. That is the error mizer made until issue #619. A test of the kernel weights cannot detect it, because the kernel had exactly the bin-integrated values derived above all along; only a grid-refinement test of the rate itself can.

For a general kernel the integrals \(\Phi^E_i[m]\) and \(\Phi^P_i[m]\) have no closed form, so mizer evaluates them once, when the kernels are built in setPredKernel(), using a composite quadrature over each bin. For the default lognormal kernel the integrand is smooth and the quadrature is effectively exact; for kernels with internal discontinuities (such as the box kernel) the bin integral correctly returns the fraction of the bin that overlaps the support. Because all of this happens at setup time, the kernel integrals have zero runtime cost: a projection performs exactly the same two FFTs per time step as before. The only run-time addition is the trapezoidal average of \((1-f_i)\gamma_i\), an elementwise operation on a species-by-size matrix.

Enabling the higher-order scheme

The higher-order quadrature is opt-in: the first-order scheme described in the earlier sections remains the default so that existing models reproduce exactly. To build the bin-integrated kernels, set the bin_average entry of the second_order_w slot,

second_order_w(params) <- TRUE

which re-runs [setParams()] and rebuilds the Fourier-transformed kernels (along with the other bin-averaged rate quadratures, so the whole model stays consistent). Because the choice lives in the slot it is preserved when the kernels are later recalculated — for example after you change a predation-kernel parameter such as beta or sigma. Set second_order_w(params) <- FALSE to switch back to the first-order scheme. See [second_order_w()] for finer control over the individual second-order schemes.

The predation-diffusion rate (used when use_predation_diffusion is TRUE) is the same prey-bin convolution as the encounter, but its integrand carries one more power of prey size, \(w_p^2\,dw_p\) instead of \(w_p\,dw_p\). Under second_order_w it therefore needs its own bin-integrated kernel with the \(\beta^{3s}\) Jacobian in place of the encounter’s \(\beta^{2s}\), \[ \Phi^{D}_i[m] = \frac{\ln\beta}{\beta-1}\int_0^1 \tilde\phi_i(\beta^{\,m-s})\,\beta^{3s}\,ds , \] which setPredKernel() precomputes and stores as ft_pred_kernel_d. For a box kernel over a fully-covered bin this evaluates to \((\beta^3-1)/(3(\beta-1)) = (\beta^2+\beta+1)/3\), the bin average of \((w_p/w_k)^2\) — the diffusion analogue of the encounter’s \((\beta+1)/2\). projectDiffusion() convolves with ft_pred_kernel_d, which in the default first-order scheme equals ft_pred_kernel_e, so the default behaviour is unchanged.

The diffusion convolution outputs at the predator node, but the transport solver needs the diffusion coefficient averaged over the predator bin (see vignette("numerical_details")). Under second_order_w, setPredKernel() therefore also folds the diffusion kernel over adjacent offsets, \(\tfrac12\bigl(\Phi^D_i[m] + \Phi^D_i[m+1]\bigr)\). This is the predator-side counterpart of the prey-bin fold of the predation kernel, and it averages the prey integral over the predator bin. The factor \((1-f_i(w))\,\gamma_i(w)\) in front of that integral varies across the same bin, so projectDiffusion() averages it trapezoidally as well (issue #619). As for predation, the product of the two averages differs from the average of the product only by an \(O(\Delta x^2)\) covariance.

Avoiding wrap-around: zero padding

FFT-based convolution is circular convolution: the grid is treated as a ring, on which the point below the smallest size \(w_1\) is the largest size \(w_K\). A sum over the part of a kernel that falls off one end of the grid therefore picks up whatever lies at the other end.

In the encounter rate this happens whenever the feeding kernel of the smallest predators reaches below the smallest resource size min_w_pp. With the default lognormal kernel, which is not truncated, that is always the case to some degree. The part of the kernel below min_w_pp should see no prey, but on the ring it sees the largest fish, as though they were prey just below min_w_pp. Larvae are then fed by the largest fish in the model. The predation rate contains the transpose of the same error: the larvae are recorded as eating the largest fish. The predation diffusion integrand carries a factor \(w_p^2\), which amplifies exactly these large-prey contributions. The size of the error depends on the model. It is negligible when the resource extends far below the kernels of the smallest fish, but in a model with min_w_pp three orders of magnitude below the egg size and abundant large fish it made the encounter rate of the larvae 9% too high and their predation diffusion several orders of magnitude too large (issue #618).

In a model of defaults edition 3 or later (see defaults_edition()), mizer avoids this by zero-padding. Let the full grid have \(K\) points, of which the fish sizes are the last \(K_w\), and let \(m_{\max} \le K - 1\) be the largest grid offset at which the kernel weights are non-zero. In the encounter rate the circular convolution wraps the term for a prey \(k\) larger than the predator \(n\) onto the kernel offset \(L - (k - n)\), where \(L\) is the length of the grid on which the FFT is taken. Because the predators are fish, \(n \ge K - K_w + 1\), and so \(k - n \le K_w - 1\). If \(L \ge \max(K, K_w + m_{\max})\), every such offset is at least \(m_{\max} + 1\), where the padded kernel is zero, and the wrapped terms vanish. The same bound works for the predation rate, where the predators \(n\) are again the fish and the wrapped terms are those with the prey \(k\) larger than the predator. When \(m_{\max} \le K - K_w\) (the kernel of even the smallest fish does not reach below min_w_pp), no padding beyond \(K\) is needed; for an untruncated kernel with \(m_{\max} = K - 1\), \(L \ge K + K_w - 1\) suffices regardless of the preferred predator/prey mass ratio, because the discrete kernel is only evaluated at the grid offsets \(0 \le m \le K - 1\). setPredKernel() therefore stores the kernels on a grid of length $L = $ nextn(max(K, K_w + m_max)), rounded up to a length whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5, for which the FFT is fast. convolve_pred_kernel() pads the prey or predator densities with zeros to the same length before transforming them. The convolutions are then linear and agree with the direct sums over the kernel to round-off.

The padded transforms are up to about twice as long as the grid. How long an FFT takes depends as much on the prime factors of its length as on the length itself, so the cost is smaller than that suggests: a projection of NS_params with the padded transforms takes about 15% longer than with the unpadded ones.

A model of defaults edition 1 or 2 keeps the unpadded transforms of length \(K\) that earlier versions of mizer used, so that its results do not change, wrapped terms included. This covers every model created with the default edition and every model saved with an earlier version of mizer, NS_params among them. convolve_pred_kernel() takes the length of the grid from the stored kernels, so the same code evaluates both kinds of model. To give an existing model the padded transforms, record edition 3 in it and recalculate its kernels:

defaults_edition(params) <- 3
params <- setPredKernel(params)

The ft_mask

Without zero-padding, the predation rate is protected from the wrap-around only by ft_mask, a logical array that is 1 for prey sizes smaller than the maximum size of the predator species and 0 above it:

return(pred_rate * params@ft_mask)

Predation on prey larger than the largest predator of a species is impossible, so this removes the wrapped contribution there. It cannot help with the wrapped contribution on prey smaller than that maximum size, and it cannot be applied to the encounter or diffusion rates at all: there the wrapped contribution lands on the smallest predator sizes, whose true rates are not zero. With the zero-padding of edition 3, ft_mask is no longer needed to suppress wrap-around. It is still applied, so that the predation rate stays zero above the maximum size of each species even if a model holds abundances there.

Kernels that are not a function of the size ratio alone

A predation kernel that depends on predator and prey size separately, rather than only on their ratio, cannot be written as a convolution. When such a kernel is supplied with [setPredKernel()], mizerEncounter(), mizerPredRate() and projectDiffusion() fall back to direct summation over the full predation kernel returned by [pred_kernel()]. That costs \(\mathcal{O}(K^2)\) operations per species rather than \(\mathcal{O}(K \log K)\), but involves no Fourier transform and so no wrap-around.
